summary:
Named after the Hindu goddess of speech—and formed from the initials of its creators, Vaibhav, Michelle, and Katie—VAMIKA reflects the vital role of clear science communication and international collaboration in solving global challenges. Inspired by NISAR, a historic joint mission between NASA and ISRO, the project demonstrates how uniting global expertise and translating complex data into accessible insights empowers communities to respond to worldwide crises.
VAMIKA is an interactive application that uses NASA-ISRO NISAR's L-band synthetic aperture radar to track and visualize flood and wetland surface change at locations worldwide — from monsoon flooding to shifting river islands.
We built a real change-detection pipeline: users compare before/after NISAR GCOV backscatter across multiple polarizations (HH, HV, VV, VH), with a draggable satellite comparison slider, multi-date time-series animation, and automated classification distinguishing open water (lower dielectric-driven backscatter) from flooded vegetation (double-bounce backscatter increase) — exploiting exactly the roughness/dielectric sensitivity that makes radar uniquely suited to flood mapping day or night, through cloud cover.
VAMIKA translates radar observations into actionable insight: it cross-references the detected flood extent with live OpenStreetMap infrastructure data to flag exposed hospitals, schools, and roads, and generates an explainable priority score and exportable Emergency Information report.
details:
VAMIKA lets a user search any location on Earth and automatically discovers real NASA NISAR L2 GCOV radar acquisitions for that area via NASA's CMR catalog. It downloads the actual before/after granules, then runs a genuine L-band SAR backscatter change-detection pipeline that classifies two physically distinct flood signatures: open water (a backscatter decrease from specular reflection) and flooded vegetation (a backscatter increase from double-bounce scattering beneath tree canopy — a signature invisible to optical satellites). Results are shown through a draggable before/after satellite comparison slider, a real multi-date backscatter time-series animation, and a map overlay of the detected flood extent. The app then cross-references that flood polygon against live OpenStreetMap infrastructure data to count exposed hospitals, schools, settlements, and roads, computes an explainable priority score, and can assemble everything into a one-click "Emergency Information" report exportable as PDF.

Benefits

SAR is the only satellite technology that can see through clouds and darkness — exactly the conditions present during most real flood disasters, when optical imagery is useless. VAMIKA makes that capability usable by non-specialists: no remote-sensing background needed to understand "this area flooded, here's how much, and here's who's at risk." Every score is rule-based and explainable (not a black-box model), and every value is either real or explicitly labeled unavailable — never fabricated — so responders can trust what they're looking at.

Intended impact

The target users are emergency managers, disaster-response NGOs, researchers, educators, and the public. The goal is closing the gap between "NASA has the data" and "a decision-maker can act on it" during the critical early hours of a flood event, while also serving as an accessible teaching tool for how SAR physics actually works.

Tools, languages, and stack

  • Backend: Python 3.11, FastAPI, Uvicorn
  • SAR/geospatial processing: h5py (NISAR HDF5 reading), rasterio, pyproj, shapely, numpy, scipy
  • Data sources: NASA CMR + ASF Earthdata Cloud (real NISAR GCOV granules), OpenStreetMap Overpass API with a Geoapify Places API fallback for infrastructure data
  • Frontend: Vanilla JavaScript + Leaflet.js, single HTML file, zero build step
  • Export tooling: html2canvas + jsPDF for the Emergency Information PDF report
  • Deployment: GCP Compute Engine (primary, persistent disk for multi-GB granules) and Render (auto-deployed fallback)

Creativity

The dual open-water/flooded-vegetation classification (rather than a single generic "flood" layer) surfaces wetland/forest flooding that most flood apps miss entirely. The priority and confidence scores are fully transparent rule-based point systems instead of an opaque ML score, so a user can see exactly why an area was flagged High priority. A curated set of "Featured Locations" are pre-computed in advance so judges/users can see a full real result instantly, without waiting on multi-gigabyte satellite downloads live.

Team considerations

Our guiding design constraint, enforced throughout, was never substitute fabricated data for missing real data — if OpenStreetMap or an infrastructure data source is unavailable, the UI says so honestly rather than inventing a plausible-looking number. We also built in resilience (multiple Overpass mirrors, a Geoapify fallback, timeout isolation so one slow data source can't block the whole report) and explicit honesty about current limitations (e.g., no gridded population dataset is integrated, so population/damage exposure is reported as unavailable rather than estimated).
